title: Suchness (section 17)
hookLine: "Tathagata" means suchness; there was nothing to receive from the past Buddha

lines: ASK ME THE FIRST THING AGAIN.
A NEW WORD AT THE CENTER.
cards: Halfway through a long conversation, a good friend sometimes says: wait, ask me the first thing again. Not because they forgot. Because everything said since has changed what the question means.
Section seventeen of the Diamond Sutra does exactly that. Subhuti asks his opening question a second time: how should one who has set out on the path stand, go on, and hold the mind?
The answer comes back with a new word at its center, and it's the name of the Buddha himself.

teach.h: THE SAME ANSWER, NO ONE LED.
teach.b: First, the repeat. The answer is much as at the start. Someone on this path should think: I will lead all beings to nirvana.
And yet, once they are led, no being has been led. A bodhisattva who holds the idea of a self is not a bodhisattva. And there is no fixed thing called one who has set out.
Long ago, under the earlier Buddha Dipankara, did he receive some thing that was the highest awakening? No, Subhuti says, and the Buddha agrees.

If there had been some thing to receive, Dipankara would not have told him: in a future age, you will be a Buddha named Shakyamuni. Because there was nothing to grasp, the prediction could be made. Third, the name.
Tathagata, the title the Buddha uses for himself, is a name for suchness, the sutra says. Suchness means things just as they are, before we add our labels, hopes and stories.
The Buddha's own name points away from a person holding a prize, toward the plain way things are. Fourth, the everyday edge.
It's the floor under your feet being exactly this floor, the rain being rain before it's ruining anyone's plans.
The sutra adds that a bodhisattva who says, I will make the buddha-lands beautiful, isn't truly one: even good work, held as my project, slips away from suchness. That's this week.
The sands of the Ganges, the ground made a shrine, the diamond that cuts, Subhuti's tears, the shoulders, the scorn: each one stripping a label off, so something can be seen as it is.

how: In Mahayana teaching, suchness (tathata) names reality as it is, without added concepts; meditators in some schools practice simply resting attention on what is present, without labeling it.

o: the polite way to address a Buddhist teacher
a calm feeling that comes after deep meditation
things just as they are, before our labels and stories

p: a name for suchness, the sutra says
said by one who isn't truly a bodhisattva

s: Subhuti asks a brand-new question in section 17
it's his opening question from section 2, asked a second time.
the Buddha received the highest awakening from Dipankara
nothing was received; that is why Dipankara could foretell his awakening.
the sutra says the name Tathagata means suchness
the Buddha's own title points to things just as they are.

games.q: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks: under Dipankara, did I receive some thing that was the highest awakening? what do you say?
o: no, there was nothing to receive
games.why: Subhuti says no, and the Buddha agrees: if there had been something to grasp, Dipankara couldn't have foretold it.

practice: Let the one thing you see as it is be the breath: feel one breath come in and go out, and notice the labels that arrive with it, too shallow, better, am I doing this right.
Let each go by like a passing car, and come back to the breath itself, cool at the nostrils, a rise, a pause, a fall. It doesn't need to be a good breath, just this one, then the next.

wordCard.voice: Suchness. Things just as they are. In section seventeen, the sutra says the name Tathagata itself means suchness. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: suchness, things as they are; section 17 links it to the name Tathagata.

carryVoice: Your line: suchness. The floor, just this floor; the rain, just rain. And that closes the week.
